title: Antibabesial treatment and persistence
definition: Antibabesial treatment means the drugs that act on the parasite itself; they are the base of treatment in every form of babesiosis, while supportive care treats the complications [R1][R2]. Persistence means infection that remains after treatment: a clinically normal carrier, a relapse, or treatment failure. It is common after treatment of the small Babesia species [R2][R3].
definition_note: The working definition was confirmed. One distinction was added from the sources: clinical cure (signs resolve) and parasitological cure (blood PCR negative) are different end points, and most drugs give the first more reliably than the second [R3][R1].
key_points: Know the species before you choose the drug: large Babesia (B. rossi, B. canis, B. vogeli) respond to diminazene or imidocarb; small Babesia (B. gibsoni, B. conradae, B. vulpes) are relatively resistant to these and are treated with atovaquone and azithromycin or a combination protocol [R2][R3].

In South Africa diminazene aceturate is the drug of first choice for B. rossi; Onderstepoort studies gave 3.5 mg/kg once [R4][R5]. Its safety margin is narrow, and a South African pharmacokinetic study advises no repeat within 21 days [R6][R1].
Imidocarb dipropionate is the reference drug for B. canis; the US label dose is 6.6 mg/kg, repeated after 14 days, and lower doses have been followed by treatment failure [R7][R8][R9].
Diminazene and trypan blue do not sterilise large Babesia infection; imidocarb at 7 to 7.5 mg/kg is reported to do so [R1].

Atovaquone with azithromycin cleared B. gibsoni below the PCR limit in 8 of 10 dogs in a placebo-controlled trial, but later case series report relapse with atovaquone-resistant cytochrome b mutants [R10][R11][R12].
Test of cure is by PCR, before treatment stops and about 2 months later, ideally twice at least 15 days apart; serology is not useful for follow-up [R3].

description.heading: What it is
description.text: The aromatic diamidines imidocarb and diminazene act well on the large Babesia species [R2][R4]. Atovaquone and buparvaquone (hydroxynaphthoquinones) act on the parasite cytochrome b and are used against small Babesia, usually with azithromycin [R2][R3]. Azithromycin, clindamycin, doxycycline and metronidazole have antiprotozoal effects; alone they reduce clinical signs but do not eliminate the infection [R3]. Trypan blue is an old drug that is still used in some parts of the world [R1].

description.heading: How common, and in which dogs
description.text: Every dog with confirmed babesiosis receives an antibabesial drug. Mildly to moderately affected dogs with large Babesia usually recover on the drug alone [R1]. In 320 dogs with B. rossi at Onderstepoort, all given diminazene 3.5 mg/kg and supportive care as needed, 10.6% died; this figure includes euthanasia [R5]. Persistence is mainly a problem of small Babesia: recurrence after treatment occurred in 11.8% of 145 dogs with B. gibsoni followed for 16 weeks [R13].

description.heading: When in the course of disease
description.text: Dogs with large Babesia usually improve within 1 to 7 days of treatment, faster than dogs with small Babesia; some take more than 15 days [R3]. In South African dogs with uncomplicated disease, the haematocrit fell by a mean maximum of 0.046 L/L, mostly at 6 to 12 hours after diminazene or trypan blue, before it rose [R14]. Carrier dogs may relapse later, when immunity falls: after splenectomy, immunosuppressive treatment or other illness [R3].

description.heading: Mechanism
description.text: Drugs that reduce parasitaemia without sterilising leave a carrier dog; in endemic areas this may maintain premunity, while in non-endemic areas sterilisation is preferred [R1]. Atovaquone binds cytochrome b. Point mutations in the cytochrome b gene, mainly M121I, are linked to relapse and non-remission after atovaquone with azithromycin [R11][R12]. Several cytochrome b mutations were also found in B. gibsoni that persisted after buparvaquone with azithromycin [R15].

species_notes.note: Diminazene is the drug of first choice in South Africa [R4]; 3.5 mg/kg was used in the Onderstepoort cohort [R5]. Imidocarb is also used [R16]. Neither diminazene nor trypan blue sterilises the infection [R1].

Imidocarb is the treatment of choice in Europe [R3]. In 49 German dogs, most that were tested by PCR became negative after the first or second injection [R17]. In one case report the dog stayed PCR-positive after 2.0 and then 5.0 mg/kg and cleared only after two injections of 9.4 mg/kg [R9].
The European review gives the same imidocarb regimen as for B. canis [R3]. Adult dogs often have mild or subclinical infection; puppies can be severely anaemic [R1].

Relatively resistant to the diamidines [R2]; imidocarb is not recommended [R4]. Atovaquone with azithromycin is first line, but relapse and resistance occur [R10][R11]. Parasitological cure is considered rare [R3].
Diminazene and imidocarb did not clear the infection in the first series [R18]. Treated dogs became PCR-negative after atovaquone with azithromycin [R19].
In a randomised trial of 59 dogs, imidocarb gave the worst results; atovaquone or buparvaquone with azithromycin did better, but neither cleared PCR-detectable infection in all dogs [R20].

criteria.criterion: Parasites on a thin capillary blood smear
criteria.threshold: Any parasitised red cell in a dog with compatible signs (B. rossi)
criteria.note: B. rossi is so virulent that one parasitised cell confirms the diagnosis. Capillary (ear margin) smears show higher parasitaemia than venous blood.

criteria.criterion: PCR on EDTA blood, with species identification
criteria.note: More sensitive than microscopy (about 50 parasites per mL against about 0.001% parasitaemia by smear) and identifies the species, which decides the drug.

criteria.threshold: PCR still positive when checked about 14 days after treatment
criteria.note: Proposed by the authors of one case report. If PCR stays positive after two injections, confirm the species by sequencing and look for co-infection and other disease.

criteria.threshold: Negative PCR before treatment stops and about 2 months after; two negative tests at least 15 days apart
criteria.note: European review recommendation. A shelter study of B. gibsoni used two negative PCRs 30 days apart, at 30 and 60 days after treatment. Blood PCR does not prove clearance from the spleen.

criteria.threshold: Return of signs or haematological abnormality with a positive smear or PCR after an initial response
criteria.note: No standard definition was found; each study used its own. This is a working definition for this page.

clinical_signs.note: Large Babesia: clinical improvement usually within 24 to 48 h; small Babesia respond more slowly.
May be clinically silent, or show persistent anaemia, thrombocytopenia or hypergammaglobulinaemia; signs can return under stress, especially in splenectomised dogs.
Salivation, vomiting, diarrhoea, epiphora, nasal discharge and pain at injection; usually short-lived.
Ataxia, opisthotonus, seizures and nystagmus with overdose; also after repeated doses.

tests.test: Thin capillary blood smear (rapid Romanowsky stain)
tests.finding: Paired pyriform large Babesia, or single small ring forms (B. gibsoni)
tests.note: Cheap and immediate. Small forms need practice; low parasitaemia (B. vogeli, chronic infection) is easily missed. Search the feathered edge.

tests.finding: Species and genotype; carrier state; test of cure
tests.note: Needed to choose the drug for small Babesia and to follow treatment. Blood PCR sensitivity is below 100%; splenic PCR is more conclusive but costly.
Shows exposure only. Healthy dogs in endemic areas can be positive, and B. gibsoni titres stay positive after treatment, so serology is not used to follow treatment.

tests.finding: Haematocrit, platelets, globulins, liver and kidney values
tests.note: Repeat until normal after treatment, especially in splenectomised dogs and with small Babesia.
Found in all samples from dogs that relapsed or did not remit after atovaquone with azithromycin in one study. Specialist or research laboratories.

differentials.distinguish: Babesiosis can be Coombs-positive and parasitaemia can be low. Examine a capillary smear and run PCR before starting immunosuppression.
Petechiae or epistaxis are rare in babesiosis alone and suggest Ehrlichia co-infection. Imidocarb did not clear experimental E. canis infection, so co-infection needs its own treatment.

differentials.condition: Mixed Babesia infection (B. gibsoni with B. vulpes)
differentials.distinguish: Only PCR separates them; 15% of dogs with either piroplasm in one US laboratory series had both.
Neurological signs after an overdose or a repeat dose; post-mortem lesions (cortical haemorrhage and oedema) resemble cerebral babesiosis.

differentials.condition: Treatment failure from the wrong species
differentials.distinguish: A large-Babesia drug fails against small Babesia. Confirm the species by PCR and sequencing when a dog does not respond.

approach.action: Confirm the infection and name the species
approach.detail: Thin capillary smear from the ear margin. Send PCR when the forms are small, the dog has travelled or was imported, or the response is poor [R1][R3].

approach.action: Weigh the dog and calculate the dose
approach.detail: Diminazene has a low therapeutic index; dose meticulously, especially in puppies [R1]. The South African label says never exceed the dose [R24].

approach.action: Large Babesia: give one antibabesial drug
approach.detail: B. rossi: diminazene aceturate 3.5 mg/kg IM or SC once [R1][R5]. B. canis or B. vogeli: imidocarb (see doses), with atropine or glycopyrrolate premedication against cholinergic signs [R3]. Do not repeat diminazene within 21 days [R6].

approach.action: Start supportive care at the same time
approach.detail: Mild to moderate cases usually need the drug only [R1]. Complicated cases need the care on the syndrome pages and usually referral (SY11).

approach.action: Small Babesia: atovaquone with azithromycin for 10 days
approach.detail: Give atovaquone with a fatty meal [R3]. Compounded atovaquone was effective in one shelter study [R21].

approach.action: Follow up and test for cure
approach.detail: Recheck haematology until normal. For B. canis, check PCR about 14 days after imidocarb [R9]. For small Babesia, PCR before stopping and about 2 months later [R3].

approach.action: Relapse or failure: re-evaluate before you repeat
approach.detail: Confirm the species, look for co-infection, splenectomy or immunosuppression [R9][R3]. After atovaquone failure in B. gibsoni, a different drug class (clindamycin, diminazene and imidocarb) has been used [R2][R12].

treatments.name: Diminazene aceturate
treatments.aim: Kill large Babesia quickly; first-line drug for B. rossi in South Africa.
treatments.evidence_summary: Standard for B. rossi in South Africa [R4]; all 320 dogs in the Onderstepoort cohort received it [R5]. In a randomised comparison in 19 South African dogs with uncomplicated disease, diminazene and trypan blue did not differ in parasite clearance or haematocrit change [R14]. In 226 Croatian dogs with B. canis, signs regressed within 24 h after diminazene, but reinfection within 30 days was seen after diminazene and not after imidocarb [R25]. It does not sterilise infection [R1] and is less effective against B. gibsoni [R3].

doses.context: Large Babesia; South African review table and the B. rossi cohort at Onderstepoort
South African product label, biliary fever in dogs
doses.note: The label states the dose as a volume, not in mg/kg. It says do not exceed the dose and do not repeat it.

doses.context: Review of B. gibsoni treatment, describing South African use for B. rossi
doses.note: Conflicts with the South African label (once, never repeat) and with the advice not to repeat within 21 days; given here because sources differ.

treatments.cautions: Narrow therapeutic index; dose meticulously, especially in puppies [R1]. Overdose causes injection-site pain and swelling, gastrointestinal signs and neurological signs [R18]. CNS toxicity can follow repeated doses because elimination is prolonged; lesions mimic cerebral babesiosis [R16]. A pharmacokinetic study at 4.2 mg/kg IM advises no repeat within 21 days [R6]; the review author notes some breeds and individuals may need a longer interval [R1].
treatments.monitoring: Clinical response within 24 to 48 h; expect the haematocrit to fall for 6 to 12 h first [R14][R3]. Watch for neurological signs.
treatments.availability: Registered in South Africa as Berenil R.T.U. (Reg. No. G2702, Act 36/1947), labelled to cure biliary fever in dogs [R24].

treatments.name: Imidocarb dipropionate
treatments.aim: Kill large Babesia, and at higher doses sterilise the infection; reference drug for B. canis.
treatments.evidence_summary: Treatment of choice for B. canis and B. vogeli in Europe [R3]. In 342 German dogs with B. canis, nearly all treated dogs received imidocarb (median 3.3 mg/kg, range 1.7 to 6.8); 87.6% of dogs with known outcome had an uncomplicated course and 6.7% died [R8]. In 49 dogs, PCR became negative after the first injection in 19 and after the second in 15; 9 were still positive after at least one injection [R17]. In US dose studies, relapses were more frequent at 1 to 2 mg/kg [R7]. In B. vulpes it was the weakest of three regimens (8 of 17 relapsed) [R20]. Not recommended for B. gibsoni [R4].

doses.context: US product label (Imizol, 120 mg/mL), B. canis

doses.frequency: once; can be repeated after 15 days
doses.context: B. canis and B. vogeli, European review
doses.note: The review suggests reconsidering the diagnosis rather than repeating if the response is poor.

doses.context: Large Babesia, reviews (South African authors)
Large Babesia, reviews (South African authors)
B. canis and B. vogeli, OIE review

treatments.cautions: Pain at injection in nearly all dogs and injection-site swelling; transient vomiting [R7]. Cholinergic signs (salivation, vomiting, diarrhoea, epiphora) [R3]. Overdose is nephrotoxic [R3]; renal tubular or hepatic necrosis [R4] and massive liver necrosis [R16] are reported; one dog accidentally given 24 mg/kg died [R7]. In the label safety study, 9.9 mg/kg twice raised ALT and AST transiently [R7].
treatments.monitoring: PCR about 14 days after treatment in B. canis [R9]. Haematology until normal [R3]. In azotaemic dogs one German clinic used lower doses (median 4 mg/kg) [R17]; no source tested dose adjustment.

treatments.name: Atovaquone with azithromycin
treatments.aim: Reduce small Babesia below the PCR detection limit; first line for B. gibsoni, B. conradae and B. vulpes.
treatments.evidence_summary: In a randomised placebo-controlled trial in 22 chronically infected dogs, 8 of 10 treated dogs had no detectable B. gibsoni DNA after treatment, against 0 of 11 on placebo [R10]. Compounded atovaquone cleared B. gibsoni in 39 of 42 dogs [R21]. Treated B. conradae dogs became PCR-negative [R19]; B. vulpes was undetectable at 90 days in 6 of 9 dogs [R23]. Relapse was frequent in Asia: 5 of 8 dogs [R11], 7 of 17 dogs [R12], and clearance in only 6 of 24 dogs in Hong Kong [R26]. In B. vulpes, 47% were still PCR-positive at 90 days [R20].

doses.frequency: atovaquone every 8 h; azithromycin every 24 h
doses.context: B. gibsoni, review table; B. conradae study (12 dogs, about 8 treated; azithromycin 10 to 12.5 mg/kg)

doses.frequency: atovaquone every 8 h with fatty food; azithromycin every 24 h
doses.context: B. gibsoni, B. vulpes; European review, US case series and Spanish trial
doses.note: The Spanish trial abstract gives 13.3 mg/kg; the full text gives 13.5 mg/kg.

doses.frequency: atovaquone every 8 h with a fatty meal; azithromycin every 24 h
doses.context: B. gibsoni, 42 shelter dogs, prospective study

treatments.cautions: Give atovaquone with a fatty meal to aid absorption [R3]. Vomiting for 2 to 3 days in 23.5% of dogs in one trial [R20]; no adverse effects in the B. gibsoni trial [R10]. Relapse can select atovaquone-resistant cytochrome b mutants [R11][R12]. Atovaquone is costly and not registered in many European countries [R4].
treatments.monitoring: PCR before stopping and about 2 months after treatment, or at 30 and 60 days [R3][R21].

treatments.name: Trypan blue
treatments.aim: Reduce large Babesia parasitaemia; an older alternative to diminazene.
treatments.evidence_summary: In a randomised comparison in 19 South African dogs with mild to moderate uncomplicated disease, trypan blue and diminazene did not differ in parasite clearance or haematocrit change, and all dogs improved [R14]. A South African review lists it as effective but notes it is used only in some parts of the world and does not sterilise infection [R1]. An OIE review says it works in dogs with mild to moderate signs [R18].

doses.duration: single dose, followed by imidocarb or diminazene 1 week later
doses.context: Large Babesia, South African review table
OIE review
doses.note: Give as a 1% solution because it irritates tissues.

treatments.cautions: Tissue irritant: strictly IV [R18][R1]. Does not sterilise the infection; its use outside endemic areas is discouraged [R1].
treatments.monitoring: As for diminazene: expect an early haematocrit fall [R14].

treatments.name: Clindamycin, diminazene and imidocarb (CDI)
treatments.aim: Clear B. gibsoni, including atovaquone-resistant strains.
treatments.evidence_summary: In a non-randomised comparison in 30 dogs with B. gibsoni, 11 of 13 dogs on CDI recovered completely and 2 relapsed, against 9 of 17 recovered and 7 relapsed on atovaquone with azithromycin; treatment lasted longer with CDI (mean 41.7 against 23.3 days) [R12]. A review states it is used for atovaquone-resistant strains [R2]. Another review reports this trial as 11 of 13 without complete cure, which conflicts with the trial abstract [R4].

doses.route: clindamycin PO; diminazene IM; imidocarb SC
doses.frequency: clindamycin every 12 h; diminazene once; imidocarb once, 24 h after diminazene
doses.context: B. gibsoni, regimen as cited in two reviews of the Taiwanese trial
doses.note: Primary paper read as abstract only; doses taken from the reviews. Mean therapy duration in recovered dogs was 41.7 days.

treatments.cautions: Carries the cautions of both diamidines (see those rows). No safety data for the combination were found.

treatments.name: Buparvaquone with azithromycin
treatments.aim: Alternative to atovaquone for small Babesia.
treatments.evidence_summary: In the Spanish randomised trial in B. vulpes, 88% of dogs on buparvaquone with azithromycin were clinically healthy at day 90, with no product-related adverse events; 68% were still PCR-positive at day 90 [R20]. In India, 8 of 12 dogs with B. gibsoni did not respond, and parasites carried several cytochrome b mutations [R15].

doses.frequency: buparvaquone 2 doses 48 h apart; azithromycin every 24 h
doses.context: B. vulpes, randomised trial (25 dogs in this arm) and European review

treatments.cautions: Well tolerated in the trial [R20]. Possible resistance in B. gibsoni [R15].

treatments.name: Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone), azithromycin and artesunate
treatments.aim: Clear chronic B. gibsoni infection and prevent relapse.
treatments.evidence_summary: In 12 Pit Bull Terriers with B. gibsoni, all were PCR-negative by day 42 and stayed negative to day 720, with no adverse effects [R27]. In an Indian trial of 20 dogs, artesunate-atovaquone-azithromycin gave more sustained remission than doxycycline-clindamycin-metronidazole [R28]. A lactating bitch given this protocol cleared infection in 3 of 5 infected puppies through the milk [R29].

doses.context: B. gibsoni, 12 dogs, Slovak case series
doses.note: The paper does not say whether 13.5 mg/kg refers to atovaquone or to the whole product (250 mg atovaquone with 100 mg proguanil per tablet).

treatments.cautions: Proguanil causes digestive upset in dogs; one review prefers atovaquone alone [R4]. No adverse effects in the 12-dog series [R27].
treatments.monitoring: PCR at 14-day intervals to day 56, then every 6 months in the series [R27].

treatments.name: Clindamycin, metronidazole and doxycycline
treatments.aim: Antibiotic-only protocol for B. gibsoni, including after atovaquone failure.
treatments.evidence_summary: Eliminated B. gibsoni from blood in 3 of 4 experimentally infected splenectomised dogs [R30]. After atovaquone with azithromycin failed, 7 of 8 dogs with recorded outcome became PCR-negative [R26]. In an Indian trial of 20 dogs, this protocol gave early improvement followed by recrudescence [R28].

doses.context: B. gibsoni, experimental study (4 dogs) and review

doses.frequency: clindamycin and metronidazole every 12 h; doxycycline every 24 h
doses.context: B. gibsoni after atovaquone failure, Hong Kong case series
doses.note: Duration was set by the clinician on PCR results.

doses.context: B. gibsoni, European review
doses.note: Lower clindamycin dose than the other sources.

treatments.cautions: Adverse effects were not reported in the case series [R26]. Antibiotics alone do not reliably eliminate infection [R3].
treatments.monitoring: PCR at about 1 and 2 to 4 months [R26].

treatments.name: Doxycycline, enrofloxacin and metronidazole, with or without diminazene
treatments.evidence_summary: In 40 dogs in Taiwan, 85.7% with diminazene and 83.3% without were judged effective (smear-negative and seven weeks in remission); diminazene did not add benefit. Efficacy was judged by blood smear, not PCR, and 6 dogs relapsed [R31].

doses.dose: 7 to 10 mg/kg + 2 to 2.5 mg/kg + 5 to 15 mg/kg
doses.context: B. gibsoni, Taiwanese case series of 40 dogs
B. gibsoni, same series (28 dogs)

treatments.cautions: No adverse effects were reported [R31]. See diminazene cautions.
treatments.monitoring: Smear-based follow-up in the study; PCR would be more sensitive [R31].

treatments.name: Low-dose diminazene followed by clindamycin
treatments.aim: Control acute B. gibsoni and prevent relapse with less diminazene toxicity.
treatments.evidence_summary: A review describes this regimen as used in Japan to reduce side effects and recurrence; it is not effective enough in splenectomised dogs [R4]. The primary study was not verified in this run.

doses.frequency: diminazene every 48 h for 3 injections; clindamycin every 12 h
doses.context: B. gibsoni, Japan, as described in a review

treatments.cautions: See diminazene cautions. Not recommended after splenectomy [R4].

treatments.name: Tafenoquine
treatments.aim: New oral option for B. gibsoni.
treatments.evidence_summary: Eight dogs with B. gibsoni, one after diminazene failure, improved rapidly; two relapsed and improved after two more doses [R32].

doses.context: B. gibsoni, Japanese case series of 8 dogs

treatments.cautions: Adverse effects were not described in the abstract [R32].

treatments.name: Doxycycline or clindamycin alone
treatments.aim: Reduce clinical signs when a specific drug is not available.
treatments.evidence_summary: A European review rates doxycycline efficacy as poor; it reduces the severity of B. canis and B. gibsoni disease. Clindamycin alone reduced signs and laboratory abnormalities in B. gibsoni. Neither eliminates the infection [R3].

doses.frequency: every 24 h, or 5 mg/kg every 12 h if vomiting
doses.context: B. canis and B. vogeli, European review
B. gibsoni, European review

treatments.cautions: Antibiotics alone will not eliminate infection; the review advises restricted use [R3].

treatments.name: Phenamidine and pentamidine
treatments.evidence_summary: In 226 Croatian dogs with B. canis, dogs given phenamidine improved more slowly than with diminazene, and reinfection within 30 days occurred, unlike after imidocarb [R25]. Pentamidine is listed among drugs used with varying success [R3]. No dose was stated in the sources read.
treatments.cautions: Only local injection-site inflammation was noted in the Croatian dogs [R25].

treatments.name: Atropine or glycopyrrolate before imidocarb
treatments.aim: Prevent the cholinergic signs of imidocarb.
treatments.evidence_summary: Reviews recommend premedication [R3][R4]; it was used in the Spanish imidocarb arm [R20]. No study tested its benefit.

doses.route: route not stated in the source
doses.context: Review of B. gibsoni treatment
doses.note: No source gave a glycopyrrolate dose.

doses.context: B. vulpes randomised trial, imidocarb arm (17 dogs)

treatments.cautions: No adverse effects of premedication were reported in the sources read.

prognosis.text: Most dogs treated for large Babesia recover: 85 to 90% survive overall, depending on the species and the level of care [R1]. Mortality, including euthanasia, was 10.6% in 320 dogs with B. rossi [R5] and 6.7% in 193 German dogs with B. canis and known outcome [R8]. With small Babesia, clinical cure is usual but parasitological cure is considered rare, and many dogs stay carriers [R3].

indicators.finding: Secondary IMHA, Rottweiler breed, red cell count below 2 x 10^12/L at diagnosis, or anaemia persisting beyond 20 days after treatment (B. gibsoni)
indicators.meaning: Higher risk of recurrence (cumulative incidence 16% to 29%).
Associated with relapse or non-remission after atovaquone with azithromycin.
Carrier dogs may relapse; follow these dogs closely.

indicators.finding: Imidocarb dose below the label range (B. canis)
indicators.meaning: Failure after 2.0 and 5.0 mg/kg in one case report; the authors advise 6.6 mg/kg and PCR 14 days later.

related.why: Triage and the order of care in complicated disease.
Transfusion and the haemolytic anaemia that the antibabesial drug does not correct at once.
Immunosuppression can trigger relapse in carrier dogs.
Diminazene neurotoxicity is a differential of cerebral babesiosis.
No source gave antibabesial dose changes for kidney failure.

evidence_gaps: No controlled trial of an antibabesial drug against B. rossi was found after the 1996 comparison of diminazene and trypan blue in 19 dogs.
How often B. rossi persists or relapses after diminazene has not been measured with PCR follow-up in the sources found.

No source gave a changed drug or dose for puppies, pregnant bitches or dogs with kidney or liver failure, beyond careful dosing in puppies; one case report treated infected puppies through the lactating dam.
The safety of giving two diamidines within 24 h (clindamycin, diminazene and imidocarb protocol) is not reported.
The dose of doxycycline for Ehrlichia canis co-infection was not verified in this run; use the ehrlichiosis guidance.
No source confirmed whether imidocarb, trypan blue, atovaquone or buparvaquone is registered or available in South Africa.
The primary Japanese study of low-dose diminazene followed by clindamycin could not be checked; its regimen is given here only from a review.

search.note: Searched for each candidate drug with canine babesiosis and each Babesia species, and for toxicity, resistance, relapse and test of cure. About 80 local treatment papers were screened; small single-centre case reports and non-PubMed regional trials without verifiable doses were left out. Some full texts were behind a paywall or a bot check and were read as abstracts.
